  1. Besides [preferred]

  From Oxford Dictionary:
  "Some people say that beside should not be used to mean ‘apart from’ and that besides should be used instead (he commissioned work from other artists besides Minton rather than he commissioned work from other artists beside Minton). Although there is little logical basis for such a view, and in standard English both beside and besides are used for this sense, it is worth being aware of the potential ambiguity in the use of beside : beside the cold meat, there are platters of trout and salmon means either ‘the cold meat is next to the trout and salmon’ or ‘apart from the cold meat, there are also trout and salmon’"

  So.. Besides and also are the same?
    ↳ **@timkurtz2953** (👍1 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQGGXZFB5Ow&lc=UgydzAKq34rzWek-gaN4AaABAg.9QQqXVQfy-09QgSaV3cs-p
      Not really.  "Besides" can be replaced by "other than".  You use it when asking someone for an answer, but you don't want them to give one specific answer.  For example, "Hey James, besides Godfather, what is your favorite movie?"  You want an answer other than Godfather.
      
      "Also" is like "in addition to".  James is funny and also pretty smart.
      
      Hope this helps.

  1. Nouns that are ideas: abstract nouns
  Anger, Intelligence, democracy
  
  When something's not concrete
  You cannot hold them in your hand, see them, or touch them but you can see examples of them
  
  Ex. I know somebody has Anger, their face is red, they're breathing heavy, they have a lot of intensity
  Those are examples of anger but not anger itself
  
  2. Nouns that describe a group of things: collective noun (the collective)
  •team •committee •crowd
  
  3. Nouns for specific things: proper
  •Toronto •Nino •Ford
  
  4. Made up of 2 words: compound 
  •dry-cleaning  •bookstore 
  Compound
  
  5. Nouns you can count on: Countable nouns
  •apples 🍏 •houses 🏡
  
  
  •pants/glasses
  -singular items (a pair of)
  
  •fish
  -singular/plural
   Fishes are like the peoples of the world

  A - one

  JamesESL:
  
  I reject 'abstract noun' as a grammatical category. There are nouns whose references are relatively abstract ('paradigm') and others and nouns whose referents are relatively concrete ('corn'). But this is an ontological distinction, not a grammatical one. (And a rather poor ontological distinction at that.) 
  
  This is a pet peeve I had at the time with how I was taught middle school english, even though I lacked the skills to formulate it at the time: being taught a dubious ontology under the guise of teaching english grammar.
  
  Unless that is, JamesESL, you can show me how nouns like 'paradigm' actually function differently in sentences than nouns like 'corn'. Do they have different morphological properties, for example? My middle school didn't teach any, that's for sure. Their distinction was roughly "things you can touch or see" versus "things that you can't". But I would be happy to be shown how there is a truly grammatical distinction      at play. Just because I am unable to imagine one doesn't mean they don't exist.
  
  Cheers.
  - Bryan

  Surround yourself with English as much as possible. Sounds simple, right? I tried this, and, oh my God, it was so difficult and discouraging in the beginning: I understood almost nothing of what was said. Then, after months of practice and lots of mistakes, I slowly began to understand more and more. It takes time. Don't think that you're stupid or that you're bad with languages if you can't do something right away. Again, It takes time. Try different things and approaches and find what works best for you.   Well James, you've helped me many times and this one wasn't the exception. Right now I'm studying for IELTS so I'm gonna share my tips with you:
  1) Right now I began to learn how to play chess so I'm reading and listening all of my lessons in English (Youtube and PDF mostly).
  2) For IELTS I pick a subject that is interesting for me (could be anything), I look for an article or digital newspaper and read it two times. On the first try, I just read for understanding the article and what it is about, and the second one I read the article looking for at least 3 or 5 new words that I have no idea what they mean. So I pick those unknown words and look for their meaning, synonyms and write one or two sentences with the new word. After that, I write a full page on what it's about the article that I've read. 
  3) The last part is a little more complicated because I don't have any native English speakers around, what I do is using an app on my phone that converts my audio notes into writing notes ("Speechnotes"). So doing this exercise I can have a certain if my pronunciation is good enough. I use some complicated words for this so I can maximize the use of this app.
  I hope you keep making some advanced classes because we really enjoy your teaching style. See you bro!

  You are talking about watching movies with or without subtitles and im not allways sure in witch language you mean on the subtitles. It is a really good step from watching at movies with subtitles in your own language to watch english movies with English subtitles. If you watch with subtitles in your own language  your brain easily gets lazy and just reads instead of listen to the english words. If you have english subtitles you get aware of the english words and expressions and you learn to hear what they are saying and how it spells. If you are streaming you can rewind and change to your own language if it is a sentence you don’t understand. Even if you easily can watch a movie or a episode without subtitles it can be good to have english subtitles sometimes because you get more aware of how they are saying things. And how words pronounce and spells.

**@rodolforobles3304** (👍0 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zwQit51uZiA&lc=UgwqYsII7XadQtcDHyF4AaABAg
  In my case, English has been a long journey. Like many other people, I started learning Englisg in school, without motivation to learn it haha, I was a child that only wanted the class to be over.
  
  When I enter college, I had to present an English exam to know if I needed to take the subject each term, and I have to admit it...I copied to avoid even 1 lesson of the language during my degree. Those 4 years without being in touch with English I thought I was intermediate, and I wrote that on my resume. What a surprise when I was interviewed for a job and I just couldn't answer properly "What is your favorite movie and why?".  THAT DAY I decided to start over, I reviewed all the tenses, basic grammar and all from the beginning.
  
  Of course I started watching a lot  of videos, and a very important tip that they all left me is "LEARN WHILE YOU CONSUME CONTENT YOU'RE INTERESTED IN ". It's amazing how that brought me the motivation I needed to keep going. I didn't stop learning because boredom wasn't part of the journey.
  
  When I felt a little bit more confident, I downloaded apps for practicing with other people, and I'm not gonna lie by telling you I wasn't a mess at first hahahah but it's just a matter of practice. That's all.
  
  Now I think I'm advanced in listening, writing and reading; and I'm working on my speaking, which I consider intermediate-advanced. 
  
  If you are reading this line, I hope my story helps you with this beautiful journey that is learning English. You'll see that sooner than you think, you'll improve your level and enjoy all the advantages that English brings with it.
  
  DON'T GIVE UP!
  
  
  p.s. Two months ago I got a job where I use English everyday because I could handle a part of the interview in English :D

    ↳ **@nursen2106** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVgmUfHGRHM&lc=UgxeBBUtbDW38GtSLch4AaABAg.9FjimlCnYWi9Fkp5SEQEH-
      I apreciate your work, but this time interestingly I find myself disagreeing with you on the very point, that made you put this lesson together. Unfortunately my comment is rather long. I hope it still can make a little impact. Please excuse my mistakes in English. 
      
       It might be very true, that some people or people in certain positions may overuse the word 'narrative'. And it might be, that it is used the same way as some people openly say 'alternative facts'. But a narrative is not a tale in a sense, that it is not to believe or a fairy tale or whatever. A narrative is the explanation (in words!) of a situation, people, the human being itself .... not using formulas or calculus. And it is a way, to set up yourself and introduce change. Narratives are very important at turning points. To explane a fact, a goal, a decision, a necessity e.g. for a whole society in words. A narrative can be a 'fake'  the same way as conclusions out of facts sometimes is. One, that just assumes, an observation at a point in time and the parameters, explains everything. In that sense facts, accounts and narratives can be the same way misleading, but they can all be precicely what is, but needs to be told and shown. 
      
      I don't want to be too philosophical (in fact, I know a bit about philosophy). But I am a social-politically interested person and did study economics and a bit sociology. As 'lay' person I was disappointed, that there are no polititians or insitutions, trying to exceed the general understanding of how economic factors have to be interpreted and decide upon, that was told (!) us from the so called neo-capitalist point of view for more than 40 years now. (which imbodied itself in the world on a global scale for about 30 years not). That moment in my live was about 10 years ago and precisely half a year later, groups of scientists started to bring into the discussion again, that we are living in a narrative about facts, that nobody dares to re-wright and we need not only new rules for decisions, but a change in the mind set - a new narrative. Away from the sense, that there is nothing else we can do, than follow facts, that come to us from somewhere out there and have nothing to do with our selfunderstanding. I know, that is going on all over the world, but speaking for the politicians in my country in Europe and our neigbours, that is the real belief-system now. And that is just not true. When today a economic scientist like Walter Ötsch (Austrian -unfortunatly very bad english accent :-D ), who knows not only how to read and operate with data, who also knows about cultural developments and shifts in avaireness etc. makes a video and speaks about the current narrative e.g. about the current crisis and it's inpact on us, about outlooks and chances etc. you will find people commenting his explanations and illustrations as non-scientific. But those comments are non-scientific themselves, because they come from a wrong understanding about what sciences outside of physics, mathematics and maybe chemistry is and can do. And it comes from an anderstanding, that a social-narrative has nothing to do in the world of hard-facts. But hard facts, as defined in physics, and ideal-facts as in mathematics. They think, the answer to a crisis can only come from the result of a calculation, and that is scientific humbug. 
      
      Even micro-econimist, that are working with model-calculation have a different world-view now. At least a lot is emerging now. I understand, that defining a narrative e.g. for a group of people only from the historic side, is problematic and that may be the cause for the feeling of 'something is not right here' - the discomfort with that word, narrative. That doesn't change, that for everybody, esp. on society level, there is always a necessity of a narrative of who we are now, how we want to live and what are our values now. We should leave space for dicussions and adjustments. Only that way we can 'calculate' our next steps. Esp. when so many people are involved and not a single individual. There is no need to 'fight' this word. The fact, that we have lost values or thrown them away and now struggle to define them new, might be uncofortable. It still has nothing to do with being fictional. Because, at it turned out so often in history, and again and again in the last 10 years. Facts, parameters can be vage as well - when it comes to set goals. And yes, I believe in facts like the landing on the moon, and that the earth is round and such :-D I don't fight facts. But I know (and I am not the only one), that there is that uncomfortable truth, that now and then, we have to set our bounderies new, so we not only kow, where we would like to go, but also, so we all know, what we are publicly talking about, when we ask for changes or that something should stay the same. 
      So the response to a narrative should be another narration, that brings into account, what you rely on and where you stand - but not the account (calculation in a broader sense). I hope, this was helpful and not confusing.

      I would recommend not to replace 'essential' with 'necessary' or 'crucial' in this context. Yes, in everyday language those words are largely interchangeable, but when talking about COVID, 'essential workers' already refers to a very specific group of people. When saying 'necessary workers', you risk being ambiguous, as people may not be sure if you're talking about the same group of workers known officially as 'essential workers', or just any group of workers who YOU believe to be necessary.

  I found a similar method by myself. It's similar like yours. The only diference is I write a short story with any word I learnt. For example, I'll use the words you've given us on this video: "Early in the morning, I was waiting my bus at the bus stop . Suddenly, a pigeon popped on my head, it made me feel so angry. Anyway, when the bus came I saw many pigeons were eating litter , I was staring that until I realized I had missed the bus. Finally, I had to take a taxi to go to the skycraper where my work is."
  
  Maybe it could take more than 5 minutes, less than 10, but I read in a neuroscience magazine when creating short stories is one of the best ways to memorize or learn because our brain make a relationship between thing and thing in this case: the new words which we are learning. I hope it helps people. It's only a short story, it shouldn't be real.

  Hey Lucy, this would be a long comment but I want you to read this and please guide me through this- 
  
  My first language is Hindi and I feel like learning a new Language and being proficient at (or in??) that language  is one of the most challenging things in the world. I think a language is almost entirely idiomatic. For example, in hindi we say "mai school me hu"- to mean I am in school but to a native English speaker that would sound like you are trying to say that you are a student (maybe someone asked you "what do you do?" And you replied "I am in school") but in Hindi it can mean both "you are at school" (you are inside that building and attending your classes) and you are in school (you are a student who studies in school) and what you mean would depend on the context. Many times, when I am not sure about something I try to translate things and that kind of messes everything up. The same way we say for e.g "Is album "me" 4 songs hai" - translation- "There are 4 songs "in" this album" but a native speaker would use "on" here instead of "in". I think a language is not just about communication but it also contours your world and how you look at things. 24/7 I am surrounded by Hindi speakers and there is NO way I would be able to speak English  confidently without being in that "english-speaking" environment. There are some nuances that I as a non-native would never understand no matter how many dictionaries or books I read. (Like that proficient in or at??)and I don't see any YouTube channel dedicated to just discussing those nuances. It's just not enough to know the meanings of a word, you have to know the contexts in which it's used and the collocations as well (for example hard and difficult means the same thing when it's about ideas and questions but would you say "the wood is difficult?"- ofcourse not) And there is no channel dedicated just to that. 
  
  What should I do? I feel like there is no other way except being surrounded by native speakers and  conversing with them but that is just not possible.

  Please don’t take this comment as some sort of criticism, Wes! I honestly appreciate your effort to help your students improve their English skills!
  
  I simply prefer the multiple choice questions, because otherwise one might come up with more than just one “correct” answer.
  
  Kind regards,
  Anna 🌺

**@gkhau6810** (👍0 · 2026-08-10) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=had-Msv2EBM&lc=UgzGf-hQG9o3R-wxSwh4AaABAg
  Thx , nice job . But we need explanation nuance  f ex. Both cease and stop mean to end an action or activity, but they are used differently.
  
  Stop is an ordinary, everyday word. It is very common and flexible.
  Stop talking.
  It stopped raining.
  We need to stop the project.
  
  Cease is more formal and often suggests that something ends completely. It is common in official, legal, military, or literary contexts.
  The company ceased operations.
  Hostilities ceased at midnight.
  He never ceased to amaze me.
  
  Grammar:
  
  Stop doing something = to discontinue an activity.
  He stopped smoking. — He gave up smoking.
  
  Stop to do something = to pause one activity in order to do another.
  He stopped to smoke. — He paused what he was doing so that he could smoke.
  
  Cease doing something / cease to do something = both structures mean to discontinue an activity.
  They ceased trading.
  They ceased to trade.
  
  Useful chunk:
  
  Cease and desist means to stop an activity immediately, especially in legal contexts.
  A cease-and-desist letter is a formal demand ordering someone to stop an allegedly unlawful activity.
  
  So, in most everyday situations, use stop. Use cease when you want a more formal, official, or literary tone.

  Over the years, I've mostly been a listener rather than someone who actively practices speaking and writing. I simply wanted to understand what you were saying, and that interest is actually what kept me going with English over the years.
  Eventually, I started paying attention not just to what you say, but to how you naturally say it. I look at your sentences, break them down, and find useful patterns I can reuse.
  This is basically what I do: 🇨🇦 Watch/listen to your videos and read the transcripts 🗣️ Shadow your English 🧩 Break down your sentences and create my own examples
  For example, I took this sentence from this lesson: "I think it's important to decide that you're going to do something so that you can get to a certain point in the future and be very happy with your progress."
  Then I look for useful patterns in it:
  🧩 so that + sentence 
  I practice every day so that I can improve my speaking.
  🧩 get to a point where + sentence 
  I want to get to a point where I can follow a conversation without thinking too much about the language.

  The methods are:
  1. Input:
   Reading fiction to understand people and their perspective
  2. Output:
  Writing to improve, modify and learn from mistakes 
  3. Pacing:
  Listening music and movies to catch the natural flow of the language and slang
  4. Mimicking: 
  Speaking like the natives
  
  BONUS: 
  1. Flash cards
  a. Write the meaning
  b. Write a sentence
  c. Write the phonetics
  d. Draw a picture 
  2. Envelope 
  Make a sentence using that word
  
  Homework:
  Practice one method each day and take a day off and repeat

  During watching a video:
  Pause each part - Read and speak the subtitle
  Resume - Listen and check you if said correctly
  Pause again if necessary - say again with the same pacing

  Can you help us how to use "due", "due on", "due by" and "due for"? I cannot barely recognize the difference between them. Thank you.
    ↳ **@PlotTwistEnglish** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VZ87Ofx4eKs&lc=UgwOay7W664xgig6yDN4AaABAg.95a3ogkWEVo96JnVKAvL_w
      due = to be planned or expected for a certain date
      
      
      due on = to be expected on, or planned for, a specific day or date (eg. due on Monday)
      due for = expected or planned for a certain date or day (same as DUE ON)
      due by = expected for a certain date, you can use it with a general time, (eg. due by next week)

I can't believe that there's no grammer rule for this, so my question to you as a native speaker is: When do I have to use not to and when to not? In sentences like: "Try not to laugh", when would I say "Try to not laugh"?
    ↳ **@singalongwithtony** (👍1 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=buoYlm_4CPk&lc=UgzUvhfpCw-yGvP9mmJ4AaABAg.91K8tqU-dew91lonWlgFcf
      Hi Michael, In my opinion, "Try not to laugh" is grammatically correct. The verb is "To laugh", there is no verb "To not laugh". We say "To not laugh" socially, as a clear and specific challenge to keep a straight (non-laughing) face. Hope that helps! Tony
    ↳ **@tchrmarta1841** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=buoYlm_4CPk&lc=UgzUvhfpCw-yGvP9mmJ4AaABAg.91K8tqU-dew97Bo1m84ExT
      It's because the verb laugh is infinitive in this sentence, when I say I laugh or she laughs the verb doens't take 'to' because it's conjugated as there is someone performing the action.

  Sir, pls makes a video about the difference between "have, had, has"
    ↳ **@MazzixG** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S7Q3XP7nvj4&lc=UgxaDEo0Di40MeWKgj14AaABAg.90NDoJZifvn90P4hQZ6R9Z
      To have is an irregular verb that means owing sth .. 
      Have in present simple doesn't change in these subjects  ( I you we you they) but (s/he it ) have becomes has so we say : 
      I have a dog
      You have a dog
      She/he/it has a dog
      You have a dog
      They have a dog 
      But in  past simple and past participle have changes to had 
      And it's used for the all the subjects 
      I/ you /she/he/it/we/you/they  .. had a dog ( in past simple )
      There are many videos that explain this so you can  check them out 
      Good luck
    ↳ **@kostantinosbardi4620** (👍3 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S7Q3XP7nvj4&lc=UgxaDEo0Di40MeWKgj14AaABAg.90NDoJZifvn90O93P_x4V-

  At 13:00, there is the sentence "Mr. E is happy because he knew Raquel would come if he would let her cook dinner." But in school, we learned that the word "would" is never a part of an if-clause. So, who is right? It would be nice to know because I'm writing my final exam (German Abitur) this year. Thanks for your help
    ↳ **@VictorMatthieu** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=Ugz01x2XkTPpDc0fwBF4AaABAg.9-s2ZEk8e739E5qMW1H0Jd
      I'm American. It sounds fine to me. I don't know if there's any sort of special grammar rule, but I've said it before. To me, it sounds extra conditional. Typically I would use it with the perfect aspect and/or probably also with the word "only", rather than just having "would" by itself. So, something like this:
      
      ". . . if only he'd have let her cook dinner." / ". . . if only he'd let her cook dinner." / ". . . if he'd have let her cook dinner."
      
      Those sound more natural to me. But, like I said, I don't know if there's some grammar rule that bans this, but honestly, most "rules" English don't really mean much and language is a very dynamic thing so you can't really usually say something is or isn't allowed. Plus with all the dialects of English (and there are A LOT), I'm sure it also depends on what type of English you're studying.

    ↳ **@follyxd** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=Ugx7eZAV8s7RAHEt3594AaABAg.90Jb85g4e5N90RXMkJTMU6

    ↳ **@VictorMatthieu** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=Ugx7eZAV8s7RAHEt3594AaABAg.90Jb85g4e5N9J5CDFZdNeb
      If there is a modal verb, you use its opposite (had -> hadn't; would -> wouldn't; will -> won't; etc). When there's no modal, you use "do". Keep the tense the same. 
      
      Your sentence is past with no modal and it's a positive statement.
      
      This means we will use "didn't"
      
      Did -> because it's a past tense main clause with no modal
      
      n't -> because the main clause is positive

**@youssefmestadi9498** (👍0 · 2020-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3Xd5FRBEx4&lc=UgyVQuLfl9whu3Pu7YJ4AaABAg

      There isn't a difference. If it's important, you can infer from context, or just ask what the person meant.
      
      He'd become a really mean person in the last few years before his death -> He had
      
      He'd become a really mean person if you let him do whatever he wants all the time -> He would
      
      He'd become a really mean person -> This is ambiguous as to its meaning; it can be either

      This structure is much less common as it can only be used with non-count or uncountable nouns (such as water, oxygen, philosophy). The article must be omitted when the non-count noun is used as an open generalisation. 
      Examples :
      All water is wet.
      I want all alcohol removed from this school.
      All sport is good for you.

      I always watch all or most videos with subtitles in Dutch / Norwegian / German etc or other target languages if I am at least intermediate level in the language, whenever subtitles are available, and when there’s no sub available, I use the ‘translate to’ option, even though it is not always 100% accurate, but most words are going to be pretty accurate tho, so it helps reinforcing them in my hern and even learning new words — I am advanced level in Dutch now, and I only learned about 5 new Dutch words from this video (luckily there are Dutch / Norwegian etc subs available) because I knew all the other words, and every time I see them, it reinforces them, which is how an automatic mode in a new language is created, and I think I am soon to develop an automatic Dutch mode, because Dutch is so easy to learn because almost all the words are so pretty (just as pretty as English words) and so distinctive, and one tends to remember prettier and more distinctive words faster (which explains why languages such as Dutch / English / Norwegian etc can be learned very fast) so, it all went super fast for me!
    ↳ **@DeShark88** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=Ugwwhi3tjQA4Nr1tF-B4AaABAg.9lhvoLscbPyA3kZodGkiIH
      Sorry, but this isn't a great summary. The key takeaway is missing, which was that speaking and listening are good to reinforce words you already know, but if you don't know a word you obviously won't say it and you also won't understand it. Whereas reading forces you and allows you to pause, look up the word, and add it to your vocabulary. You can do this at a surface level, only looking up words that prevent your understanding, or you can do it intensively, whereby you actively study a text sentence by sentence, study it's makeup and structure and then cover it up and re-create it from memory.
    ↳ **@DeShark88** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=Ugwwhi3tjQA4Nr1tF-B4AaABAg.9lhvoLscbPyA3k_4iVzs21
      All the stuff about lingq, or however it's spelt, was to show you that importing ebooks allows you to very easily use the online dictionary to define words you don't know. Whereas some languages (like Chinese) has awful dictionaries where finding definitions is a slog, online learning permits rapid look-ups which makes learning more fun, which makes learning more likely.

**@GandalfTheWise0002** (👍14 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=Ugwx8rOCY8rsbrj6p6R4AaABAg
  I've found that combination of intensive and extensive reading effective as well.  In addition, I do something partway in between I think of as targeted reading.  If there is a particular aspect of the language that is frustrating me when I run across it, I target it each time I encounter it until it is not frustrating.  The first time I tried it, I had hit a plateau in Ancient Greek in my extensive reading.   I had improved quite a bit, but just seemed to not get any better.  Intensive reading wasn't effectively fixing this either.   It was an issue of internalizing grammar to the point it was automatic.
  
   I don't remember why, but I decided to fix one problem at a time.  The first obvious problem was that I hadn't internalized verb endings of the indicative cases to the point they were completely automatic.  To fix this, during extensive reading, I paused at each indicative (and subjunctive verb), thought about it intentionally for a bit, then picked up again with extensive reading at the beginning of that sentence.  I found that quick emphasis on a particular aspect of the language helped internalize it.  Within a few days, the verb endings were not much of a problem so I stopped focusing on them.
  
  I've found that this targeting of the aspect of grammar that is most annoying and frustrating applies the Pareto Principle to clearing out the worst stumbling blocks to comfortable extensive reading.  I don't stay on one aspect until I have it perfect, but rather until it's not a noticeable impediment to smooth extensive reading.   This is something that is much like what using parallel texts, interlinears, or computer click-for-definition functions is for vocabulary when extended reading, except it's for grammar.  It's a momentary distraction to the reading, but gives a quick  review on what is needed.   
  
  I found targeted reading a great addition to both intensive and extensive reading.  It's a minor temporary slowdown to extended reading that gives a permanent bump up in skills.  I've found that this targeting usually clears most stumbling blocks in a few days or at most a week without turning all my reading time into intensive reading.

  I love reading and look forward to doing it extensively in my target language (Japanese) but I’ve heard from many sources that reading a lot without doing a lot of listening upfront can harm your pronunciation. With Japanese this particularly important because if you develop bad habits with regard to pitch accent, as well as general pronunciation, it will be difficult to correct later on. Also, reading tends to be easier than listening, so there will be a comprehension gap unless you do a lot more listening than reading. I’m currently focusing on doing intensive listening for a year before I really jump into reading. I’d be curious to hear others’ thoughts on this.

**@nathanlaoshi8074** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgwatajV8jnawIcWn2Z4AaABAg
  Problems with looking up every unknown word:  1) it takes forever, 2) you might "guess" the wrong meaning for words with multiple definitions, and 3) it makes the entire exercise very disjointed.  This is where Krashen comes in:  if you have a mostly comprehensible text, context will help the student "guess" more accurately than looking up the word, and the flow is maintained.  Of course, you have a limited selection that way, and if the content is not compelling enough, motivation to power through is tough to come by.
  
  Personally, I prefer a hybrid approach:  I read whatever the heck I feel like reading, ignore most of the unknown vocab (many words will become clear enough with time), and only look up words used in at least five instances where I think meaning is being obscured by not knowing them.  This technique worked for me in French, German, and Italian, and is working just fine in Spanish.  Mandarin is more challenging; I have yet to arrive at a technique for that one.
    ↳ **@saikougenz** (👍0 · 2025-12-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgwatajV8jnawIcWn2Z4AaABAg.9tPdGeCPCh_AQUoEriTanl
      but you have to start somewhere, so it’s fine for beginners to keep look things up until they reach a level where they can infer the meaning of a word from surrounding words and context.

    ↳ **@Thelinguist [channel author]** (👍2 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgyqdUzrrOB-SQVshAp4AaABAg.9l_9eVC1xW79l_OwJNwxV2
      When I begin there are lots of blue words which become yellow. Since I start with the mini-stories, there is so much repetition that many become white (known). As I progress into more difficult material there are fewer blue words, altho at least 10-15%. But this also improves. Yellow words should gradually convert to white because you see them so often or move them manually to known.
    ↳ **@anaxluisa** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgyqdUzrrOB-SQVshAp4AaABAg.9l_9eVC1xW79lbMl_pAomq
      That's totally normal, especially if you're learning a language from scratch! People go about it differently, but as Steve mentioned, once you repeat the lessons and progress through them, you can manually change the level of yellow words (from 1 to 4), so they will gradually become white.
      
      I started Korean on LingQ from a lower beginner level with the Mini Stories, and I would say 95+% of the words I read where yellow in any given lesson, but as I continued moving forward and complementing that study with reading from other courses in a similar difficulty stage as well, I quickly started seeing that number decrease as I got exposed to the same words over and over again.
      
      Again, people go about it differently, but I change the number on a yellow word every time I can guess the meaning, so they gradually become white. If at some point I can't recall it that's not a big deal, I just move it back to yellow. The important thing is to keep reading from different materials at a similar level, because that way you get exposed to both new and repeated words, and that makes it easier to understand new blue words through context. After two months, most of what I read went from 95% to 55% new words, which is a massive improvement. I can now (very slowly) read webtoons, which was inconceivable when I started with the language.

    ↳ **@Rudolphhhhhh** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkSpBCP17EY&lc=UgzY0BFJMbuIJWsp4uB4AaABAg.9l_zwPgT7RT9laDZtn2UVh
      Nonsense. First of all, Alphonse Daudet is not François Rabelais: aside from some archaic words or sentence structure, at least 90% of the vocabulary and grammar that is used in those short stories, are usable nowadays in French. Then, everyone should know that in each language in the world, the language used in books, even in the new ones, is not really the language that is actually spoken. For example, even today, we are using "passé simple" tense in French novels, but almost never in spoken language. So, it is the learner that has to be clever enough to know that the vocabulary and grammar used in books are not always usable in real life: to know that, he has to vary the different contents of reading (the old ones as well as the new ones) and compare that with the reality of real conversation with French natives (knowing that even among native French people, not everyone speaks the same way, e.g. social network's jargon filled with a lot of invasive English words, or young Arabic native people who are living in the suburbs, this is definitely not the French I speak).
      
      Then, it is like the Japanese language that is spoken in anime: people tend to say that we definitely have to avoid learning Japanese from anime, because it is supposed to be too rude. But it is also a big mistake to think like that, because actually, there are much more usable vocabulary and grammar in those anime that not usable ones. So, it is the learner that has to be clever enough to discover by himself what is actually usable of not in real life without shocking native people, thanks to conversations and diversification of what he reads and listens.
      
      In other words: diversification, diversification, and diversification.

  Thanks for the video, Steve! However, I don't agree that reading is the best way to build vocabulary. I don't understand why you are so adamant in denying the effectiveness of the cards. Yes, reading is a great way to find the words you need, but it's always faster and more efficient to learn them through cards, provided it's done correctly. The cool thing is that this method allows you to transfer words immediately into passive vocabulary. I've also heard you say that it takes a lot of time to come up with associations, but that's also a matter of skill - I can do it in a few seconds, but I'm sure I'll remember the words forever. Besides, you don't have to come up with associations yourself - there are a lot of ready-made associations for different words on the web, and if you make your own, you can also put them on the web to help other people.       @Asrashas  Currently I'd say I'm at a low intermediate level in Japanese. My vocab is lacking quite a bit but I know at least 500 kanji, probably closer to 800 or something (I don't really keep track).
      The radicals that make up a kanji can give a clue to its meaning and/or its reading.
      泳 (swim), 注 (pour) and 波 (wave) all have meanings related to water, and all have氵at the side, which is a form of the radical for water.
      The kanji 亡 can be read as ぼう (bou).
      望, 忙 and 忘 all contain 亡 as one their radicals and have ぼう as one of their readings.
      So once you know a decent amount of kanji, it becomes a lot easier to pick others up because of this.
      There have been times where a word had a kanji I didn't know, but I was able to work out the kanji reading based on the radicals. Then when I put together the reading of the whole word, I realised I already knew it, but it was a word I had only heard spoken and never seen written down.
      So yes, you definitely need more knowledge for this in Japanese compared to some other languages, but it's maybe not as bad as you think.
      I think a few hundred kanji would be a good starting point to jump into reading. And you only need to learn the meanings, since it's much better to learn the kanji readings by just learning the words they're used in.

  The biggest problem that I've with a new language is the sound of the letters.
  
  Not to mention not all languages uses latin as base.
  
  Say, I'd be diving on russian or whatnot. 
  IF I learn first the sound of letters, then I can read anything on the screen, answer correctly, and also start practicing my pronunciation from vowel to vowel, letter by letter.
  It's quite a simple concept, when we start in school, this is exactly the very first thing we're exposed to, before we can learn how to write and read, and thus speak.
  
  
  I haven't tried many language tools yet, and definitely haven't given enough time... 
  Duolingo, babbel, talk pal, memrise. 
  
  From those, memrise leagues ahead of anything else. I need to the learn the very foundation, before I can actually learn words.
  For instance, when a tried a new language on duo, I had to memorize word by word, and on top of that, try to also make a memory from the sound of each word... Which is obviously inefficient and dumb. From memrise, it's not required, because I'd get the foundation to "how to read" from the get go. And then I can learn words, without having to memorize each word. I can have a good idea about the pronunciation, without having to practice word by word, because I know how each letter is meant to sound. 
  
  IDK, maybe I am biased, but I just don't get it... Yeah, Talk Pal would get me faster into speaking with natives... But at same time, I'd be a illiterate, not knowing how to write, read and having to waste a lot of time to memorize  word by word. 
  
  I'll give a try to your recommendations but... I think the best case scenario is.
  Memrise for base and foundation, then talk pal or speak (haven't tried) to further practice pronunciation through conversation. Anyways...

**@kalevipoeg6916** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qgUIa-Vbxs8&lc=UgyO9McEcdquu3DEKyB4AaABAg
  Here's the problem with you "trying" 47 language learning tools: 
  because the objective is to see which one leads you to fluency, scientifically speaking the only REAL way of doing that would be to choose dozens of people with roughly the same level of intelligence, same age bracket, similar levels of motivation and focus and to have THEM learn the same language with English as their native tongue (to eliminate the variable of mother tongue making it easier or harder), all of them being monolingual so there's no linguistic cross-pollination going on  - and you have them use the apps for let's say 1 year, every day for a set amount of time with a set number of lessons - so that nobody is spending 5 hours a day while the other guy spends 30 minutes a day which warps results - and from THERE you can can them tested in their proficiency level - reading, writing, listening comprehension and speech output, vocabulary level, etc. - and THEN you can say something useful about the apps. UNTIL then it's all anecdotal at best - "I feel like I gained more from this one". ALSO, if you're learning the same language from multiple apps, you've already tainted your results because even a LITTLE bit of learning from one makes it harder to gage the results of the other. 
  
  My suggestion is, maybe constrain it to the top dozen language learning tools, find a couple dozen volunteers willing to do this with you (some WILL drop out along the way, humans are like that, so backups are necessary) and get a baseline on them as monolinguals with a DESIRE to learn language but no experience in actually doing so, and follow up with them - maybe even add incentives if they make it the full year and make sure they're ONLY doing the app and nothing else, for a set amount of learning time each day. 
  
  THEN you compare the results with the SAME language and the same MOTHER tongue - English, let's say, learning Chinese, a VERY distant language. 
  
  The added complication is that even within the same program different language courses may have different results just depending on how that method clicks for each person but it's a START. 
  
  I'd love to see a video from you in a year or so with exactly this kind of experiment - because that's ACTUALLY valuable data.

  Definitely your way of learning languages is by listening since you don't like to memorize words and dramatically see the structure of the word. For me, that is something that I do use, but I really like to see templates, solve sentence exercises, order words, but something that I really like. is that you show me the explanation of how the word is pronounced. **@JenniferSpanish** (👍1 · 2026-06-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJBP34upuAM&lc=UgzTF-KqtKv0KRyuYs14AaABAg
  Absolutely! I'm doing a lot of reading now in Spanish (I've been using the Dreaming Spanish method of listening). I probably should've started reading much earlier since I'm hearing impaired, and it's harder for me to follow fast Spanish, or pick up words being used. 
  
  I've spent 5 1/2 months so far of intensive reading, and not only has my reading stamina gone up, I've been noticing tons of little words throughout each book. Including escalofrío (like the French equivalent in the video). Even noticing grammar tenses have become much, much easier. The le/se/me/te words before/after a conjugated verb aren't confusing me as much, and I'm starting to pick out root words too, but only if I read it slowly. Although, the funny thing about reading C1/C2 level books is, I'll sometimes come across a word in Spanish and when Iook up the meaning in English, it's some obscure word I've never heard of, or it's the same obscure word. I've seen 2 like this in a C1 level book I'm reading right now. For the B1/B2 level books I'm reading, I'm really starting to notice that snowball effect.
  
  On the speaking part, I've been trying that more. I'm 49, so I'm kind of old-school, and there's that old habit that's like, "If I don't have correct, proper grammar, the whole thing will be marked wrong!". But, I'll try to say something and check it, and it'll be on the right track (maybe an accent was off, or a tense was off, or words were re-ordered). One thing that I'm probably going to try and do is, after reading a paragraph of a book, try to describe the gist out loud in basic Spanish (A2/B1 level).
  
  With the C1/C2 level "challenge books" as I call them (yeah, maybe 20% of words are unknown), I'll read 1 chapter without looking anything up, seeing what I can make of the gist, then I look at a translation of the chapter, then I go through a paragraph or two slowly to pick out words I've seen occuring a few times (lately, I've been trying to describe the word using simple Spanish), then re-read that paragraph without stopping. I liken it to a video game where you're fighting a tough final boss or a tricky level. The first time, it might take 4 hours, then you look up how to beat it (i.e., the translation), then play it again, and your brain is like, "Ah yes, I remember you! You did X and Y and I need to do A and B". Only with reading it's like, "Ah yes, I remember escalofrío from that previous book! So, this must be a tense/uneasy situation the character is going through".
  
  With flashcards, the only time I've ever used them was 26 years ago learning Kanji (Tuttle Kanji Cards), but I would also say the kanji out loud, too. Personally, my ideal flash card would be:
  
  Front: TL word. 3-5 comprehensible sentences.
  Back: (bold, white text) Definition of the word in A2/B1 level (or 1 level below the word's CEFR level). Personal note (small font, blue text) to give me a hint. Same background/foreground answer (for a spoiler text) containing the English word.

**@user-albsim** (👍1 · 2026-06-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJBP34upuAM&lc=UgxOxdeyMPWXAr5ga6B4AaABAg
  For what it’s worth, I think the brain operates in completely different modes when learning vocabulary.
  
  1) Translation mode
  This is common among beginners. A foreign word is mentally translated into the native language before meaning is accessed.
  
  2) Association mode
  At a later stage, the brain begins reinforcing links between words and concepts directly. Meaning becomes connected to images, tastes, experiences, situations, and emotions. Semantic neural networks are gradually built.
  
  3) Chunk mode
  The learner no longer processes language word by word. Entire phrases, sentence patterns, and complex expressions are stored and retrieved as semantic units.
  
  4) Simulation mode
  At this stage, the learner begins to think in the foreign language. The language is used for inner dialogue, planning, emotions, and spontaneous perception. Reactions become increasingly automatic and immediate.
  
  5) Anticipation mode
  The brain develops a predictive readiness. It begins anticipating which structures, expressions, or grammatical patterns best fit a particular communicative purpose.
  
  6) Concept mode
  Thinking of a concept directly evokes linguistic patterns in the target language, without conscious translation. Language becomes tied to abstract thought itself.
  
  What I want to emphasize is that learning vocabulary is not merely about creating associations that “make sense.” Many language courses seem to assume that forming a simple mental link is sufficient — for example, imagining yourself walking down a creepy lane in Paris to remember a word.
  
  But what matters more than merely creating a link is attaching meaning or weight to the word. Emotional relevance appears to strengthen retention far more deeply than arbitrary association alone.
  
  The brain does not simply connect a word to an image. It connects significance to the word — in other words, the brain treats the word as important.

  Flashcards have never worked for me. 
  I like learning vocabulary but I hate these cards with German on one side and the other language like Spanish, French or Turrkish ON THE OTHER SIDE.
  Nope for me. I need to see German PLUS the other language at the same time to memorize it.
  And I started long time ago to organize my vocabulary in Excel with Categories and I chose the topic I am interested in.
  I am working at my Turkish right now and I have an alphabetical list of words I do not need that often.
  Topics I am interested in get a separate tab like cooking.
  I put the words in the long alphabetical list in categories like, people, countries, cities, animals, nature. Some with sub categories.
  I work with colors a lot.
  All verbs do have a yellow background. I copy the WhatsApp emojis in the cell with the word or photos from the internet which gives me context.
  This works pretty good for me.
  Often I go through my alphabetical list and notice words are missing which I know in addition.
  I have friends in Turkey and last time I visited my friend actually forgot that I do not understand everything because on household things or shopping for food you can talk to me and I understand everything and I can respond properly.
  I try to watch Turkish tv every day and I love that they have several quiz shows about words. I use those to broaden my vocabulary.
  Sometimes I write down the answers where I do not know the words.
  Since 2 months I suddenly can understand more of the questions and sometimes I know the correct answer even before the candidate.
  Usually on topics where I already have picked up more words.
  Last week I watched  a movie "The Lost City" with Sandra Bullock, Channing Tatum and Brad PItt in Turkish and undestood maybe 75%. Without knowing the movie before in English or German.
  I might not be the most structured learner.
  I also use Duolingo to repeat certain words that actually in daily life my friends do not use but I hear them on tv a lot.
  Ah and next month my most favorite cooking copetition will start again.
  They alternate with some other show and I am really curious how much I will understand now after 6 months of break.
  So for me getting context on vocabulary is easiest watching tv as there is stuff on any topic. News, food, art, travel, animals, nature, history.... it just lies there....

But the way linguists like Language Jones described them: whole phrases or short sentences that are relevant to your life or that you learned from the context of real conversations in your target language. This is one of the most effective ways to move knowledge OF the language into the category of procedural knowledge, so that you can actually use grammar and vocabulary correctly on demand. It’s actually quite effective and it avoids all the pitfalls that he mentioned, as long as it’s done with spaced repetition. There are ideas that we all want to be able to express about our lives or about the world without waiting to find that sentence in a reader or transcript.

      Thanks a lot for submitting your WFAD response! You did a great job, and it’s clear from your writing that you’ve been practicing daily.
      
      There were a couple of language mistakes, but they don’t interfere with the meaning, so you shouldn’t worry too much about them. For example, low-income and high-income jobs are written with a hyphen, and the phrase “so that human capital does not continue to be damaged” sounds a bit unnatural.

      However, what I would do to improve the score is: 
      1. Write it as one complete paragraph.
      
      2. Avoid referencing the students’ opinions. Don't read them so you don't waste time. This way, even if you choose a similar idea, you will still explain it in your own words, making it different from what the students wrote. Try this approach and see how much better your writing improves. You might begin with: "While I appreciate the points made by both students, I strongly believe that..." Then, proceed with your explanation and example. That’s the only reference to the other students you need.
      
      3. Make sure you provide details for the sentences you write. For instance, provide an example of how the government can intervene right after the sentence where you discuss it. Otherwise, great job, and best of luck with your prep!

      While I understand Sofia's perspective on stifled economic growth due to government intervention, I agree with David. I think that such intervention is necessary to improve our society. Instead of hiring human actors, companies big and small are all utilizing cheap, accessible Al to generate videos. As a result, even highly skilled workers are no longer being hired, (comma) and their jobs are being increasingly taken over by automation. With government support, we could foster an environment that benefits from technological advancements, but is not overthrown or overshadowed by them.

**@JWinch** (👍1 · 2026-08-09) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCnw3sCyEb0&lc=UgwymxOsF9p4KkHyziV4AaABAg
  I can't speak for the general academic field, but I think the situation in AI/ML research may differ from the circumstances that led to the recommendations in this video. One of the findings in my SLR (no SLR AI usage), currently in peer review by 5 reviewers at a top 10 AI journal (Artificial Intelligence Review), is that the AI/ML field may not do systematic literature reviews often enough. I didn't even filter to PRISMA systematic literature reviews when I found ~3% of NLP papers and closer to 1% of Computer Vision papers were systematic literature reviews. Anecdotally, of this SLR's 8 nearest neighbors, only 2 used a non-ad hoc method: 1 PRISMA and 1 a method I wasn't familiar with. There are several reasons behind this, which I detail in the paper.
  
  The consequence became a main finding in the SLR: I reviewed dozens of papers claiming state of the art whose authors and reviewers seemed unaware that the state of the art had actually been reached 5 years earlier, or why. So I'm doubtful that reviewers of AI/ML papers will require all the things mentioned in the PRISMA guide, even though these authors are arguably better positioned than most to actually do them. In many other fields, authors might not be familiar with some of those terms, or know whether the AI they chose could provide them. (No diss on those authors; it's genuinely nerdy stuff that AI vendors tend to shield users from.)
  
  We're using a lot of AI on my second SLR, bridging the bleeding-edge/What Me Worry? attitude of AI/ML with a field that traditionally values PRISMA/PROSPERO (though it's not medical, which helps). But it is not making decisions; it only gives recommendations. And it does save time in many ways.
  
  Given the limited interest in lit reviews in the AI/ML field, I'm seriously considering extending the AI-enhanced SLR tools I built for my 2nd SLR and offering them to the AI/ML community, to take the biggest pain out of lit reviews so people do more of them, stop reinventing the wheel, and find actual research gaps. I believe that, at least in AI/ML, the field could benefit from more AI (applied well, using good tools like the FastTrack Claude integration you continue to enhance, thank you; what I'm building for SLRs, and what others I saw at EACL 2026 are building) to help people manage information overload, avoid repeating others' mistakes, and find useful results faster.

**@kparag01** (👍4 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgxB6yNqm17bvUNRkIZ4AaABAg
  is it secured to use through MCP ?
    ↳ **@profdavidstuckler [channel author]** (👍3 · 2026-07-29) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgxB6yNqm17bvUNRkIZ4AaABAg.AZjQVTO6MPvAZjUr3k7ij_
      Yes. The connector is read-only. It only receives the search query Claude sends it, and the only thing it returns is published paper metadata (titles, abstracts, citation counts, links) from the databases. There’s no account, no login, nothing to store so it never sees your name, email, files, or anything else in your conversation. Traffic is encrypted and because requests reach us via Claude’s servers, we can’t even see your IP address, so the searches arrive effectively anonymous. The one sensible habit, as with any search engine, is to put research topics in your queries, not personal details.

**@AnotherproblemOn** (👍2 · 2026-07-31) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgwO0-g-1uEeZIyoDYN4AaABAg
  Amazing, i will try it out to see how it compares to consensus. Thank you so much.
    ↳ **@profdavidstuckler [channel author]** (👍1 · 2026-07-31) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zzAFnqioNzc&lc=UgwO0-g-1uEeZIyoDYN4AaABAg.AZtG-AAejJAAZtOYF-Ux8-
      Super let me know what you think. Consensus is good at what it does, which is answering a question with a search. Ours does something different. It runs named methods, the Duplication Test, gap saturation, citation trajectory, inside a conversation, so you can narrow one question over ten or fifteen linked queries rather than one search at a time. And it deliberately won’t tell you your idea is good. It hands you the papers with DOIs and the method to judge them, because the judgement is the skill your examiner is testing. I built it the way I check my own topics. Use both if you like. Ours is free.
